title: SafeChat: Building AI-Powered Safety Systems at Scale in a Real-Time Marketplace

themes.theme: LLM Unit Economics at Hot-Path Volume

insights.claim: Calling a frontier LLM on every item in a high-volume hot path is economically and operationally unworkable: at roughly 4 million chat messages per day, per-call LLM pricing and 2-10 second average latency made the naive 'just ask an LLM if it's safe' design a non-starter.
insights.speaker: Bruna Pereira
insights.so_what: Consumer-scale real-time products cannot monetize LLM inference at list price on every event; the addressable spend for LLM vendors in hot paths is a small filtered slice, not total traffic.
insights.quote: For our use case, we have like 2 to 10 seconds in average of latency for each of these calls.
insights.locator: When we first talked about it, the first response

insights.claim: A cheap self-hosted classifier in front of the LLM removes over 90% of traffic before it ever reaches a paid model, which is the only reason the economics of LLM moderation close at scale.
insights.speaker: Bruna Pereira
insights.so_what: The durable spend pattern is hybrid: cheap owned inference for volume plus expensive vendor inference for the hard residual, capping how fast per-token vendor revenue can scale with user traffic.
insights.quote: Because the economics, they only work if you ask only the hard questions to the LLM.
insights.locator: if you have a hot path with high volume

insights.claim: Internally trained models are 'cheap' specifically because their cost structure is fixed deployment plus one-off training rather than per-call, with the SafeChat classifier retrained nine times and still amortized across 4 million calls a day.
insights.speaker: Bruna Pereira
insights.so_what: Cost advantage of in-house models grows superlinearly with volume, so the highest-traffic AI applications are structurally the most likely to insource inference away from vendors.
insights.quote: It's like a one-time cost for 4 million calls a day.
insights.locator: How cheap it is depends on the volume

insights.claim: The commercially available moderation API that seeded the training data was too slow for production use, serving only as an offline labeling instrument rather than a runtime dependency.
insights.speaker: Bruna Pereira
insights.so_what: Off-the-shelf safety APIs may capture data-labeling budget without capturing the far larger real-time inference budget.
insights.quote: we used this moderation API that we have available on the market, which is super slow. That's why it does not work for us.
insights.locator: Was the cheap model ever super deterministic

insights.claim: Asking an LLM for a multi-axis severity score rather than a safe/unsafe boolean produces materially more stable outputs, because scoring plays to what LLMs are good at while binary judgments collapse ambiguous context into an unreliable flag.
insights.speaker: Bruna Pereira
insights.so_what: Prompt-output schema design, not model choice, is where reliability gains come from — a cheap lever that reduces pressure to buy larger models.
insights.quote: Do not ask the LLM for a Boolean. Instead, ask the LLM for a score.
insights.locator: This is the slide that I want you to remember

insights.claim: Scores are architecturally superior to labels because they allow thresholds to move, new categories to be added, and graduated actions to be taken without rebuilding the system.
insights.speaker: Bruna Pereira
insights.so_what: Systems built on continuous outputs can be retuned as policy or regulation shifts, avoiding costly re-architecture — a real option value in a moving compliance environment.
insights.quote: because a Boolean is a flag and a score is a knob
insights.locator: Do not ask the LLM for a Boolean

insights.claim: Severity scores map directly to escalating business remedies: low severity gets the message censored, mid severity gets it blocked, high severity blocks it and offers a free order cancellation, and very high severity cancels the order, warns the offender and removes the affected party from the interaction.
insights.speaker: Bruna Pereira
insights.so_what: Safety scoring translates into refund and cancellation liability, so model calibration is a direct P&L variable, not just a trust metric.
insights.locator: This is why the score is important as well

insights.claim: Precision in the score itself is illusory — asking an LLM for a fine-grained numeric rating misreads what the model is doing, since it reasons rather than calculates.
insights.speaker: Bruna Pereira
insights.so_what: Teams over-engineering numeric LLM outputs will get false confidence; coarse scales are the defensible design.
insights.quote: don't ask it for a 5-digit score because the LLMs are not calculating anything, they are reasoning
insights.locator: When using LLM, do not ask for labels

insights.claim: Two months spent instrumenting chat and characterizing the data before building anything determined the entire architecture, because the finding that only a small single-digit percent of messages were unsafe is what justified an aggressive cheap first-pass filter.
insights.speaker: Bruna Pereira
insights.so_what: The base rate of the target class dictates whether a tiered architecture pays off; buyers evaluating AI vendors should ask for that number first.
insights.quote: Only a small single-digit percent of messages were unsafe.
insights.locator: When we ran this analysis, we confirmed

insights.claim: The data-understanding phase is the step teams most want to skip, and skipping it makes model cost irrelevant because an uncharacterized dataset yields nothing regardless of which model is applied.
insights.speaker: Bruna Pereira
insights.so_what: Time-to-value for enterprise AI is gated by data instrumentation, not model availability — a structural drag on adoption timelines.
insights.quote: This is the boring step that everyone wants to skip.
insights.locator: This is the boring step

insights.claim: The first training round produced a near-binary model because the only available examples were extreme cases surfaced through complaints; gradation only emerged after a second round labeled with a third-party moderation API.
insights.speaker: Bruna Pereira
insights.so_what: Complaint-sourced training data is severely biased toward extremes, a failure mode that silently caps model usefulness in any escalation-driven dataset.
insights.quote: The first round of training that we had, it was like a bunch of really bad messages and a bunch of ok messages. The model was a bit of almost binary.
insights.locator: Yes, the cheap model is scored also

insights.claim: Model gaps are discovered through human escalation rather than automated monitoring, with the most recent retrain triggered by abbreviations that the cheap first layer waved through before the LLM ever saw them.
insights.speaker: Bruna Pereira
insights.so_what: Tiered filtering creates blind spots invisible to the expensive layer, so human-in-the-loop review remains a permanent operating cost, not a transitional one.
insights.quote: It doesn't matter if the LLM understands the abbreviation because it never reached there because the first layer says, of course, it's safe.
insights.locator: First, we did random analysis on the data

insights.claim: Marketplace interactions lasting only six to forty minutes remove the relationship history that social platforms rely on for moderation context, forcing immediate action on single messages.
insights.speaker: Bruna Pereira
insights.so_what: Moderation tooling built for social graphs does not transfer to transactional marketplaces, creating a distinct product category rather than an addressable extension.
insights.quote: different from a social media platform, we don't get to build strong relationships between these parties
insights.locator: When we talk about safety, a meaningful amount

insights.claim: The chat latency budget is a fraction of a second per message, which is the binding constraint that ruled out synchronous LLM inference and set the sub-100ms p90 requirement for the in-house classifier.
insights.speaker: Bruna Pereira
insights.so_what: Latency, not accuracy, is the gating spec in real-time safety, favoring small owned models over API-served frontier models regardless of quality gap.
insights.quote: It had to be fast and respond in less than 100 milliseconds at 90%.
insights.locator: Then we built a small classifier

insights.claim: Voice moderation is structurally weaker than chat moderation because by the time audio is transcribed and analyzed the recipient has already heard the words, so the only available intervention is post-hoc — hanging up the call or cancelling the order.
insights.speaker: Bruna Pereira
insights.so_what: Real-time voice safety cannot be made preventive with current latency, so voice-channel risk stays a remediation cost rather than a preventable one.
insights.quote: For voice, at the moment that we transcribed the message and analyzed it, the words were already heard by the recipient.
insights.locator: I talked about chat, but for voice and image

insights.claim: The platform processes over 4 million chat messages, more than 400,000 consumer-Dasher calls, and over 200,000 images per day across chat and SMS.
insights.speaker: Bruna Pereira
insights.so_what: Concrete throughput figures set the denominator for any per-call pricing model quoted to a marketplace of this size.
insights.quote: we have over 4 million messages exchanged in chat every day
insights.locator: Talking about scale, we have over 4 million

insights.claim: The deployed system delivered roughly a 50% reduction in safety incidents driven by verbal abuse, framed explicitly as harm reduction rather than a model accuracy metric.
insights.speaker: Bruna Pereira
insights.so_what: A halving of abuse incidents is the kind of outcome metric that justifies sustained safety headcount and defends against regulatory and litigation exposure.
insights.quote: This number is not like a model accuracy improvement that we had. This is real reduction in human harm.
insights.locator: After we did that, we measured how many incidents

insights.claim: The working SafeChat system was deliberately thrown away once other teams asked for their own versions, on the reasoning that the reusable asset was the cheap-then-expensive-then-graduated-action pattern rather than the application built on it.
insights.speaker: Bruna Pereira
insights.so_what: Recognizing when demand is for the pattern rather than the product is the trigger for platform investment — and mistaking one for the other multiplies maintenance cost.
insights.quote: What they wanted was the pattern that we created.
insights.locator: We noticed that if we started to implement

insights.claim: The resulting platform is content-agnostic by design: it owns decision logging, model-provider integration and conditional step orchestration, while client teams supply the domain meaning.
insights.speaker: Bruna Pereira
insights.so_what: Separating orchestration from semantics is what lets one team serve safety, fraud and content-guideline use cases without linear headcount growth.
insights.quote: The teams, they bring the meaning and the platform orchestrates that.
insights.locator: We built a content-agnostic moderation platform

insights.claim: Cheap code generation makes reuse harder to justify at the moment of building, but maintenance cost is unchanged — the argument for platforms strengthens rather than weakens as coding gets cheaper.
insights.speaker: Bruna Pereira
insights.so_what: Cuts against the thesis that AI coding tools reduce the value of shared internal platforms; the ongoing cost base, not authorship, is where the money goes.
insights.quote: It's cheap to create code, it's not cheap to maintain the code.
insights.locator: I noticed that today it's so cheap to create code

insights.claim: Demand pulled the platform well beyond safety into profile picture moderation, signup name screening, food review moderation and fraud detection in chat and phone calls.
insights.speaker: Bruna Pereira
insights.so_what: A single moderation primitive spans trust, content and fraud budgets, so internal platforms can absorb spend that would otherwise go to several point vendors.
insights.locator: When we started rolling out SafeChat

themes.theme: Build vs Buy and Vendor Orchestration

insights.claim: The platform supports three model classes — internally trained and hosted models, contracted external vendor models, and external prompts routed to any vendor LLM — with commodity capabilities like image safety deliberately bought rather than rebuilt.
insights.speaker: Bruna Pereira
insights.so_what: Mature AI buyers segment by commoditization: they insource high-volume differentiated inference and buy solved problems, compressing vendor pricing power in the middle.
insights.quote: For example, image safety is something that is already solved. We don't need to build it all over again.
insights.locator: We have the external models

insights.claim: An internal LLM gateway sits between the platform and all outside providers, letting client teams pick target models and declare fallback and retry strategies without writing code.
insights.speaker: Bruna Pereira
insights.so_what: Gateway abstraction commoditizes the underlying model vendors and makes switching a configuration change, structurally eroding provider lock-in.
insights.quote: The LLM gateway is actually a very important piece of this platform.
insights.locator: We have the external prompts

insights.claim: Fallbacks are model-class-agnostic: when internal servers fail the system falls back to a slower external vendor, and a failing vendor can be backstopped by an LLM, though not for chat where volume is prohibitive.
insights.speaker: Bruna Pereira
insights.so_what: Degraded-mode design implies steady-state multi-vendor contracts kept warm purely for availability, a hidden recurring cost line in AI infrastructure budgets.
insights.quote: It's slower, but it's better than nothing.
insights.locator: Actually, one thing that I didn't mention here

insights.claim: Provider outages and malformed structured outputs are treated as routine operating conditions, handled by declarative retry counts and a structured error returned to the client.
insights.speaker: Bruna Pereira
insights.so_what: LLM reliability is still low enough that production architectures budget for failure by default, adding integration cost that offsets headline API pricing.
insights.quote: if you've already used LLM models, you must know that sometimes they just are not responding
insights.locator: We can use the features that are available

insights.claim: Model training and fine-tuning are explicitly out of scope for the moderation platform and owned by a separate ML platform team, with the moderation platform acting only as a client of already-trained models.
insights.speaker: Bruna Pereira
insights.so_what: Large organizations are splitting AI into a model-production layer and an application-orchestration layer, which is where tooling budgets will separately accrue.
insights.quote: the training and retraining and fine-tuning part is something that is totally handled by the ML platform team
insights.locator: Does your platform also help with automating

insights.claim: Backtesting against historical data with human labeling is built into the platform as a gate before production, applicable to a whole agent or to any individual step.
insights.speaker: Bruna Pereira
insights.so_what: Evaluation infrastructure is becoming a first-class platform feature rather than an ad hoc script, defining a distinct tooling category.
insights.quote: It's terrible to go blindly with some prompt to production to see what happens when you throw it there.
insights.locator: The backtesting is super important as well

insights.claim: Evaluation set size is bounded by human attention rather than statistics: past about a thousand examples reviewers answer carelessly and the resulting scores degrade.
insights.speaker: Bruna Pereira
insights.so_what: Human labeling throughput is the hard ceiling on eval quality, which is why automated or model-graded evaluation is the next bottleneck to be sold into.
insights.quote: If I had to throw a number, I would say a thousand is a good number.
insights.locator: Did you come up with any way to quantify

insights.claim: How much evaluation is enough depends on the gray-area density of the use case: unsafe messages are clearly unsafe, whereas fraud signals like promising to pay on arrival are often benign tipping behavior.
insights.speaker: Bruna Pereira
insights.so_what: Fraud detection carries far higher false-positive cost than safety moderation, so the same architecture will not deliver comparable accuracy across use cases.
insights.quote: For fraud, for example, there are things that are pretty fraud-y, but then they are not in the end.
insights.locator: That's hard. I'll give you an example

insights.claim: Taxonomies drift with observed complaints — the category set was expanded to include disrespect after most escalations reaching humans turned out to be about disrespect rather than outright unsafety.
insights.speaker: Bruna Pereira
insights.so_what: Category schemas are living artifacts, so systems whose outputs are hard-coded to fixed labels accumulate rework debt as policy evolves.
insights.quote: You need to keep looping and improving it.
insights.locator: When we started, we had only a few data

insights.claim: Sync and async moderation agents represent a latency-versus-complexity tradeoff: synchronous execution is reserved for gating decisions like blocking a chat message, while asynchronous execution publishes results to a Kafka topic and allows more and heavier steps.
insights.speaker: Bruna Pereira
insights.so_what: Only the small share of decisions that must gate an action pay the latency tax, letting richer and more expensive analysis run off the critical path.
insights.quote: We use synchronous only when we want to gate a decision.
insights.locator: Your moderation agent, it can be of two different types

gist: DoorDash engineer Bruna Pereira details SafeChat, a tiered moderation architecture where a sub-100ms in-house classifier clears over 90% of 4 million daily chat messages and only ambiguous cases reach an LLM that returns multi-axis severity scores rather than a safe/unsafe boolean, cutting verbal-abuse safety incidents roughly 50%. Once other teams asked for their own versions, the team discarded the working system and rebuilt the underlying cheap-filter-then-LLM-then-graduated-action pattern as a content-agnostic, no-code moderation platform spanning internal models, vendor APIs and an LLM gateway with backtesting.
